mainTopic: Does יאוש make a thief the owner? Plus why the four- and five-times payment applies only to an ox and a sheep.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a proof that יאוש (the owner giving up hope) does not make a thief the owner. A stolen animal, like a blemished one, can never be fixed for a קרבן. רבא brings another proof from the word קרבנו, 'his offering.' Since before יאוש this would be obvious, the verse must mean after יאוש, which shows that יאוש does not acquire. The גמרא settles a contradiction in רבא's words: either he changed his mind, or רב פפא said one of the statements. Next, the גמרא asks why the four- and five-times payment applies only to a שור or שה, and not to a חיה or עוף through a word-link to שבת. רבא answers that the פסוק names 'ox and sheep' twice. After testing several options, the גמרא finds that the 'שור' at the end and the 'שה' at the beginning are the extra words. Finally, רב rules that after יאוש a second thief pays double to the first thief. רב ששת rejects this and begins a proof from רבי עקיבא, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A stolen animal has no fix, before or after יאוש
steps.stepSummary: The end of an earlier proof: a stolen animal, like a blemished one, can never become fit, whether before or after יאוש.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too a stolen animal has no fix. It makes no difference whether it is before the owner gave up hope or after.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a proof it already started. A stolen animal is compared to a blemished animal: neither one can ever be fixed for a קרבן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A blemish never goes away, so the comparison means a stolen animal also stays invalid no matter what. If it stays invalid even after יאוש, then the thief never became its owner through יאוש.

keyTerms.meaning: A fix or remedy; a way to make it valid
The owner giving up hope of getting back what was stolen

phrases.english: so too a stolen animal has no fix;
no difference whether before despair,
and no difference after despair.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a proof begun before this section.
steps.raayaObject: יאוש does not transfer ownership to the thief
steps.raayaSupportSource: Comparison of a stolen animal to a blemished animal, which can never be fixed

steps.title: רבא brings a proof from the word 'his offering'
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the proof comes from קרבנו: it must be his own offering, not a stolen one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: the proof is from here. 'His offering,' and not a stolen one.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא offers a different source for the same idea. The word קרבנו, 'his offering,' rules out a stolen animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By itself this source does not yet say anything about יאוש. The next steps will show why it must be talking about after יאוש.

keyTerms.meaning: From here; introduces a new source
An offering brought in the בית המקדש

phrases.english: Rava said: from here:
"His offering", and not a stolen one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A different source for the same conclusion as step 1.

steps.title: When is the verse needed? Before יאוש it would be obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which case the verse is about, and shows it cannot be before יאוש, since that needs no verse.
steps.simpleTranslation: When is this? If you say before יאוש, that is obvious. Why would I need a verse?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what case the verse is about. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before יאוש, the animal clearly still belongs to the owner, so the thief cannot offer it. A verse would not be needed for something that obvious, so the verse must be about a different case.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need a verse?

phrases.english: When?
If you say before despair,
it is obvious; why do I need a verse?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks which case רבא's verse is talking about.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the verse refer to before יאוש or after יאוש?

steps.title: The verse is about after יאוש, so יאוש does not acquire
steps.stepSummary: The verse must be about after יאוש, which proves that יאוש does not make the thief the owner. The גמרא agrees.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't it after יאוש? So learn from this that יאוש does not acquire. Yes, learn from this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא concludes that the verse is about after יאוש. It agrees that this proves יאוש does not give the thief ownership.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If יאוש made the thief the owner, the animal would be 'his offering' and allowed. Since the verse still forbids it, the thief is still not the owner after יאוש.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from this; we can prove it

steps.whatToRemember: According to this proof, יאוש alone does not make a thief the owner of what he stole.

phrases.english: Rather, is it not after despair?
So learn from this that despair does not acquire?
Yes, learn from this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3 and draws the conclusion.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: יאוש לא קני: the owner giving up hope does not transfer ownership to the thief.

steps.title: רבא seems to contradict himself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: didn't רבא himself say this source is about stealing another person's קרבן?
steps.simpleTranslation: But wasn't it רבא who said that this is about someone who stole his friend's קרבן?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a contradiction in רבא's words. Elsewhere he explained this same kind of source a different way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the source is about stealing an animal that was already a קרבן, then it is not about an ordinary stolen animal at all. In that case it proves nothing about יאוש, which goes against what רבא just said.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it true that...; opens a challenge
Of his friend; belonging to someone else

phrases.english: But wasn't it Rava who said
that it is about one who stole his friend's offering!
phrases.notes: רבא said this earlier to push away a similar proof: the animal was already a קרבן when it was stolen.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether רבא could have made the proof in steps 2-4.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Elsewhere רבא explained the source as being about a stolen קרבן, which would make it useless as a proof about יאוש.

steps.title: Either רבא changed his mind, or רב פפא said one of them
steps.stepSummary: Two answers: רבא took back one statement, or one of the two statements was really said by רב פפא.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say he changed his mind. And if you want, say that רב פפא said one of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the contradiction. It gives two possible answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Answer one: רבא held both views at different times and took one of them back. Answer two: the two statements came from two different people, so there is no contradiction at all.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say; introduces one possible answer
He took it back; changed his mind

phrases.english: If you wish, say: he retracted,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: חַד מִינַּיְיהוּ רַב פָּפָּא אַמְרַהּ.
phrases.english: and if you wish, say: Rav Pappa said one of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Retraction, or the statements belong to different speakers
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא held two opposite views at once.
steps.terutzMaskana: Either רבא retracted one view, or רב פפא said one of the statements.

steps.title: Returning to the משנה: the four-and-five payment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule that תשלומי ארבעה וחמשה applies only to a שור or a שה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: the rule of paying four or five times only applies to a stolen ox or sheep.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה about the four-and-five payment. It is setting up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה limits this extra penalty to a שור or a שה. That limit is the target the next step will question.

keyTerms.meaning: The fourfold or fivefold payment a thief pays if he slaughters or sells a stolen animal
Etc.; the rest of the quote is in the משנה

phrases.english: And the rule of fourfold and fivefold payment
etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of יאוש and stolen קרבנות ended in step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Fourfold and fivefold payment applies only to a stolen שור or שה.

steps.title: Why not include wild animals and birds through a word-link to שבת?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why we don't learn a גזירה שוה from the word שור by שבת, where חיה and עוף are included too.
steps.simpleTranslation: But why limit it? Let us connect the word 'ox' here to the word 'ox' by שבת. There, wild animals and birds count like an ox, so here too they should count like an ox.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה's limit. It suggests a word-link to שבת that would widen the law to more animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By שבת, the word שור is not limited to oxen, since חיה and עוף are also included. If the same word here is linked by a גזירה שוה, the four-and-five payment should also apply to stealing a חיה or עוף. That clashes with the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching that links two places in the Torah that use the same word
Like them; the same as them

phrases.english: But why?
Let us learn 'ox'–'ox' from Shabbat
phrases.notes: The שבת פסוק is דברים 5:13, which lists 'your ox' among the animals that must rest.

phrases.aramaic: מָה לְהַלָּן חַיָּה וְעוֹף כַּיּוֹצֵא בָּהֶן,
phrases.english: just as there, wild animals and birds are like them,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כָּאן חַיָּה וָעוֹף כַּיּוֹצֵא בָּהֶן!
phrases.english: so too here, wild animals and birds should be like them!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the limit stated in the משנה in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule limiting the four-and-five payment to שור and שה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A גזירה שוה on the word שור from שבת would widen the law to include חיה and עוף.

steps.title: רבא: the verse repeats 'ox and sheep' to limit the law
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the פסוק says 'שור ושה' twice, which shows only a שור and שה are included.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: the פסוק says 'ox and sheep' two times. That means: ox and sheep, yes; anything else, no.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends the משנה. He shows that the פסוק itself blocks the word-link to שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the פסוק names שור and שה twice, the extra mention is read as a limit: only these animals. A clear limit in the פסוק is stronger than the גזירה שוה, so חיה and עוף are left out.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for why the extra penalty applies only to a stolen שור or שה, and not to other animals.

phrases.english: Rava said: the verse says:
'ox and sheep,' 'ox and sheep,' two times –
phrases.notes: שמות 21:37 names the ox and sheep once at the start and again at the end.

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹר וָשֶׂה אִין, מִידֵּי אַחֲרִינָא לָא.
phrases.english: ox and sheep, yes; anything else, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting extra wording in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A גזירה שוה from שבת would include חיה and עוף.
steps.terutzMaskana: The repeated 'שור ושה' limits the law to these two animals only.

steps.title: Which mention of 'ox and sheep' is the extra one?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which of the two mentions of 'שור ושה' is really extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: which one is extra?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא checks רבא's claim by asking which mention of 'ox and sheep' is the extra one. This sets up the test that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's answer only works if one mention is truly not needed for its plain meaning. So the גמרא has to find which one that is.

keyTerms.meaning: Extra; not needed for its plain meaning

phrases.english: They say: which one is extra?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the basis of רבא's answer in step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which of the two mentions of שור ושה in the פסוק is the extra one.

steps.title: The second 'ox and sheep' is not extra
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tests whether the second mention is extra and shows it is needed. Without it, we would think the thief pays nine animals for each one he stole.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the 'ox and sheep' at the end is extra, because the Torah could have written: 'If he steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters it or sells it, he shall pay five cattle in its place and four sheep in its place.' But if the Torah had written it that way, I would think he must pay nine animals for each and every one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries out one option: maybe the second mention is the extra one. Then it rejects that option.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the end of the פסוק just said 'in its place' without naming the ox and the sheep, we could not tell which payment goes with which animal. We might think the thief pays both five cattle and four sheep, nine in total, for every animal. So the second mention is needed, and the extra mention must be somewhere else.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say; introduces a suggestion that will be tested

steps.confusionAlert: The quote here is not the real פסוק. It is a made-up version the גמרא uses to show why the real wording is needed.

phrases.english: If you say the 'ox and sheep' at the end is extra,
since the Torah could have written:
'If he steals an ox or a sheep
and slaughters it or sells it,
he shall pay five cattle in its place
phrases.notes: The real פסוק says 'in place of the ox' and 'in place of the sheep.' Here the גמרא imagines a shorter version.

phrases.english: and four sheep in its place';
if the Torah had written it this way,
I would have thought he must pay nine
for each and every one!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the first possible answer to the question in step 10 and rejects it.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the second mention of 'שור ושה' is the extra one.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Without naming the animals at the end, the פסוק could be read as requiring nine animals for every theft, so that wording is needed.

steps.title: The Double 'For It' Could Prevent the Mistake
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the claim that the second 'שור ושה' is needed. In the shorter wording, 'תחתיו' would appear twice, and that could already teach five for an ox and four for a sheep.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you will say: but it is written 'for it', 'for it', so one 'for it' is extra.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on step 11. It argues that we would not make the 'nine animals' mistake, because the word 'תחתיו' (for it) would be written twice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 said that without the second 'שור ושה' we might think the thief pays nine animals for each one. Here the גמרא says that if nine were meant, 'תחתיו' would only need to be written once. The extra 'תחתיו' would show that each payment goes with its own animal, so the second 'שור ושה' might really be extra after all.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say (introduces a possible objection)
Is extra (not needed for its simple meaning, so it comes to teach something)

phrases.english: And if you will say
but it is written 'for it', 'for it'
phrases.notes: He means the shorter wording from step 11, which would say 'five oxen for it, and four sheep for it.'

phrases.english: so one 'for it' is extra

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא הָא כְּתִיב תַּחְתָּיו תַּחְתָּיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rejection in step 11 by suggesting another word in the shorter wording would block the mistake.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 11's claim that the second 'שור ושה' is needed to avoid the 'nine animals' mistake
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The double 'תחתיו' would already show that the payments are separate, so the second 'שור ושה' is not needed for that.

steps.title: 'For It' Is Needed for the Quality of the Payment
steps.stepSummary: The double 'תחתיו' cannot be used, because a ברייתא learns from it that the thief may not pay with lean, low-quality animals.
steps.simpleTranslation: That word is needed for another teaching, as it is taught in a ברייתא: You might think that if he stole an ox worth a מנה, he may pay five lean animals for it. So the פסוק says 'for it', 'for it'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The double 'תחתיו' is already being used for a different lesson, so it cannot also block the 'nine animals' mistake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא learns from 'תחתיו' that the animals he pays must be like the stolen animal in quality. Since 'תחתיו' is busy with that lesson, the second 'שור ושה' is still needed, and step 11's point stands.

keyTerms.meaning: A different teaching learned from the פסוק
A sum of one hundred דינרים
The פסוק teaches us to say

phrases.english: That word is needed
for another teaching, as it is taught in a ברייתא:
You might think that if he stole an ox worth a מנה,
he may pay five lean animals for it?
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets, 'five', is added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: So the פסוק says: 'for it', 'for it'.
phrases.notes: 'For it' means the payment must match the stolen animal, so cheap lean animals don't count.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 12 by showing that 'תחתיו' is already used for a different teaching.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The word in question is needed for a separate דרשה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The double 'תחתיו' is extra and could block the 'nine animals' mistake.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'תחתיו' teaches that the payment must equal the stolen animal in quality, so the second 'שור ושה' is still needed.
steps.whyThisMatters: This closes off the option that the second 'שור ושה' is extra. It sends the גמרא to look at the first mention instead.

steps.title: Suggesting the First 'Ox and Sheep' Is Extra
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the first 'שור ושה' is the extra one, since the פסוק could have mentioned the animals only at the end.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the 'ox and sheep' at the beginning is extra, since the Torah could have written: 'If a man steals and slaughters it or sells it, he shall pay five oxen for the ox and four sheep for the sheep.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now tries the other option for the question in step 10. It says the first mention of 'שור ושה' could have been left out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ending of the פסוק already says 'for the ox' and 'for the sheep', so it is clear which animals were stolen. That makes the 'ox or sheep' at the start look unneeded, so it can teach that only these animals are included.

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, meaning the Torah
And slaughters it and sells it

phrases.english: Rather, the 'ox and sheep' at the beginning is extra
since the Torah could have written:
'If a man steals, and slaughters it or sells it,'
phrases.notes: The real פסוק (שמות 21:37) says 'If a man steals an ox or a sheep'; this version just drops those words.

phrases.english: he shall pay five oxen for the ox,
and four sheep for the sheep.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Since the second mention turned out to be needed, the גמרא tries the first mention.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The first 'שור ושה' is extra, because the פסוק could have said the animals only at the end.

steps.title: Worry That the Thief Must Steal Two Animals
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that without the first 'שור ושה', we might think the payment applies only if he stole and slaughtered both an ox and a sheep.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the Torah had written it that way, I would have said: not until he steals two animals and slaughters them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the suggestion from step 14. It argues that the first 'שור ושה' may be needed after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the shorter wording, the end of the פסוק mentions both 'the ox' and 'the sheep' together. A reader might think the thief only pays four and five after stealing and slaughtering two animals, one ox and one sheep. The first 'שור או שה' would show that one animal is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have thought (a mistaken first idea)

phrases.aramaic: אִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא הָכִי, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא:
phrases.english: If the Torah had written it this way, I would have said:
not until he steals two animals and slaughters them!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא הָכִי הֲוָה אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the suggestion in step 14 by showing a possible misreading of the shorter wording.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the first 'שור ושה' is extra
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Without the first mention, the פסוק might be read as requiring the theft and slaughter of two animals, so the first mention is needed.

steps.title: 'Slaughtered It' Shows One Animal Is Enough
steps.stepSummary: The word 'וטבחו' (and slaughtered it) is singular, so one slaughtered animal is enough. For now, the suggestion that the first 'שור ושה' is extra survives this challenge.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written 'and slaughtered it', meaning one animal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The singular word 'it' already shows that the thief pays even for one animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since 'וטבחו' already tells us that one slaughtered animal is enough, the first 'שור ושה' is not needed to teach that. This keeps step 14's suggestion alive for now. The next steps raise more challenges, and step 21 will show that the first 'שור ושה' is needed after all.

phrases.english: It is written 'and slaughtered it', meaning one animal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 15, so step 14's suggestion survives for now.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Another word in the פסוק already blocks the mistaken reading
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without the first 'שור ושה', one might require the theft and slaughter of two animals.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'וטבחו' is singular, so slaughtering one animal is enough. This challenge does not show that the first 'שור ושה' is needed.

steps.title: Maybe he must steal and sell both animals
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that without the first 'שור ושה', we might think the payment applies only if he stole and sold both an ox and a sheep.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say: he only pays if he steals both of them and sells them both!
steps.whatsHappening: Step 16 showed that slaughtering one animal is enough. Now the גמרא asks the same question about selling: maybe he must steal both animals and sell both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'וטבחו' answered the slaughtering case, but the פסוק also speaks about selling. If the first 'שור ושה' were left out, someone could still think the selling case needs both animals. That would make the first 'שור ושה' necessary again.

keyTerms.meaning: But say (a challenge offering another way to read the text)

phrases.english: But say: not unless he steals both of them
phrases.notes: Both of them means an ox and a sheep.

phrases.english: and sells them!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵימָא: עַד דְּגָנֵיב תַּרְוַיְיהוּ וּמְזַבֵּין לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same kind of challenge as Step 15, this time about selling instead of slaughtering.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 14 that the first 'שור ושה' is extra.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Without the first 'שור ושה', the פסוק might be read as needing both animals to be stolen and sold, so those words would be needed.

steps.title: The word 'ומכרו' means one animal
steps.stepSummary: The word 'ומכרו' (and sold it) is singular, so selling one animal is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written 'and sold it' — this refers to one animal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge: the פסוק says 'sold it', not 'sold them', so one animal is enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works just like 'וטבחו' in Step 16. The singular ending shows that the selling is of one animal, so we do not need the first 'שור ושה' to teach this.

phrases.english: 'And sold it' is written — about one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Proof from a singular word in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He must steal and sell both an ox and a sheep.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'ומכרו' is singular, so selling one animal is enough.

steps.title: Maybe he must slaughter one and sell the other
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a mixed case: maybe he pays only if he steals two animals, slaughters one, and sells the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say: I would think he only pays if he steals two, slaughters one, and sells one!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a new reading. Each verb is singular, but maybe the פסוק means one animal slaughtered and a second animal sold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 16 and 18 showed that each verb is about one animal. That still leaves room to say the two verbs are about two different animals. If so, the first 'שור ושה' would be needed to rule this out.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have thought (a mistaken first idea)

phrases.english: But say: I would have thought
not unless he steals two,
and slaughters one and sells one!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵימָא: הָוֵה אָמֵינָא עַד דְּגָנֵיב תְּרֵי, וְטָבַח חַד וּמְזַבֵּין חַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After both singular verbs were explained, the גמרא suggests they might refer to two different animals.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the first 'שור ושה' is extra.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Singular verbs still allow a reading of one slaughtered animal plus a second sold animal, so the extra words might be needed to rule this out.

steps.title: The word 'או' means either action alone
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says 'או מכרו' (or sold it), so either slaughtering or selling alone is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written 'or sold it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the פסוק uses 'or', so he does not need to do both actions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Or' shows that slaughtering and selling are two separate choices. Either one alone brings the payment. There is no need to slaughter one animal and also sell another.

phrases.english: 'Or sold it' is written.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Proof from the word 'or' in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He must slaughter one animal and sell another.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'או' shows that either slaughtering or selling alone is enough.

steps.title: Maybe he must steal both and leave one
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a case the singular verbs and 'או' do not answer: he stole both animals, then slaughtered or sold only one and kept the other. So the first 'שור ושה' is needed after all.
steps.simpleTranslation: But still I would have thought: he only pays if he steals both, and slaughters one and leaves one, or sells one and leaves one!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows a reading that none of the earlier answers can rule out. Because of this, the first 'שור ושה' cannot be the extra words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here only one animal is slaughtered or sold, so 'וטבחו', 'ומכרו' and 'או' all fit. But the theft would still be of both animals. Only the first 'שור או שה' (an ox OR a sheep) teaches that stealing one animal is enough. So those words are needed, and the idea from Step 14 falls apart.
steps.confusionAlert: This challenge is different from the earlier ones. The earlier ones were about the slaughtering or selling. This one is about the stealing: maybe he must steal both, even if he only slaughters or sells one.

phrases.english: But still I would have thought
not unless he steals both of them
and slaughters one and leaves one,
or sells one and leaves one!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַכַּתִּי הֲוָה אָמֵינָא עַד דְּגָנֵיב תַּרְוַיְיהוּ וְטָבַח חַד וּמְשַׁיַּיר חַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the earlier answers do not cover every case, so the approach of Step 14 cannot stand.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 14 that the first 'שור ושה' is the extra wording.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Without 'שור או שה' at the start, we could think he must steal both animals, even though he slaughters or sells only one. So those words are needed and are not extra.

steps.title: A new answer: the end 'שור' and the start 'שה' are extra
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes its approach. The extra words are 'שור' at the end of the פסוק and 'שה' at the beginning, as the shorter wording it suggests shows.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: 'ox' at the end and 'sheep' at the beginning are extra, since the Merciful One could have written: 'If a man steals an ox and slaughters it or sells it, he shall pay five cattle in its place, and four sheep in place of the sheep.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer. It rewrites the פסוק in a shorter way to show which two words could have been left out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the shorter פסוק, 'שור' stays at the start and 'שה' stays at the end, so each animal is still named once. The end 'תחת השור' becomes just 'תחתיו', and 'או שה' at the start is dropped. So this answer does not cut out the whole first 'שור ושה', and the problem from Step 21 does not arise.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (a new approach replacing the old one)

phrases.english: Rather: 'ox' of the end
and 'sheep' of the beginning are extra,
for the Merciful One could have written:
'If a man steals an ox and slaughters it or sells it,'
phrases.notes: This is not the real פסוק; it is a shorter version the גמרא makes up. Compare שמות 21:37.

phrases.english: 'he shall pay five cattle in its place,'
'and four sheep in place of the sheep';

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces Step 14's approach, which Step 21 knocked down.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which words of the פסוק are really extra?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The 'שור' at the end and the 'שה' at the beginning, since a shorter פסוק could still name each animal once.

steps.title: Only an ox and a sheep get the four- and five-times payment
steps.stepSummary: Since the end 'שור' and the start 'שה' are not needed, they teach that the four- and five-times payment applies only to an ox and a sheep, not to anything else.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need 'ox' at the end and 'sheep' at the beginning? Learn from this: an ox and a sheep, yes; anything else, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the extra words are there and gives the final lesson they teach.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the Torah repeats words it did not need, the repeat comes to teach something. Here, naming ox and sheep again stresses these two animals only. So the four- and five-times payment does not apply to stealing any other animal or item.
steps.whatToRemember: Final answer: the extra words are the 'שור' at the end and the 'שה' at the beginning of the פסוק. They teach that ארבעה וחמשה applies only to an ox and a sheep.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the limit of the law: a thief who slaughters or sells any other stolen item pays only the regular double payment, not four or five times.

phrases.english: 'Ox' of the end and 'sheep' of the beginning — why do I need them?
Learn from this:
an ox and a sheep, yes,
anything else, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״שׁוֹר״ דְּסֵיפָא וְ״שֶׂה״ דְּרֵישָׁא לְמָה לִי? שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the lesson from the extra words found in Step 22.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The four- and five-times payment applies only to an ox and a sheep; other stolen items do not get it.

steps.title: The משנה: one who steals from a thief does not pay double
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה. A person who steals something that was already stolen does not pay תשלומי כפל.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who steals after a thief does not pay the double payment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting the משנה's rule about a second thief. This quote sets up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a thief pays double (כפל). The משנה says that if someone steals an item from a thief, the second thief does not pay that double payment. He only returns the item or its value.

keyTerms.meaning: One who steals from a thief, a second thief
The double payment a thief owes

phrases.english: One who steals after a thief does not
pay the double payment.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין הַגּוֹנֵב אַחַר הַגַּנָּב מְשַׁלֵּם תַּשְׁלוּמֵי כֶפֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the end of the שור ושה discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A second thief who steals from the first thief is not liable for כפל.

steps.title: רב limits the rule to before the owner gives up hope
steps.stepSummary: רב says the משנה's rule applies only before יאוש. After יאוש the first thief owns the item, so the second thief pays כפל to the first thief.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב says: They taught this only before the owner gave up hope. But after the owner gave up hope, the first thief acquired the item, and the second thief pays double to the first thief.
steps.whatsHappening: רב explains when the משנה's rule applies. He says it only covers a theft from the first thief before the owner gave up hope.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the owner gives up hope of getting the item back (יאוש), the first thief legally acquires it. So the second thief has stolen from its legal owner and must pay him כפל.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this in the case of...
The owner's giving up hope of getting the item back

steps.confusionAlert: רב is not saying the second thief pays the original owner. After יאוש, he says the double payment goes to the first thief.

phrases.english: Rav said:
They taught this only before despair,
phrases.notes: Despair here means the owner gave up hope of getting his item back.

phrases.english: but after despair,
the first thief acquired it,
and the second thief pays the double payment
to the first thief.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא לִפְנֵי יֵאוּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the משנה's rule quoted in step 24.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Before יאוש the second thief is not liable for כפל. After יאוש the first thief owns the item, and the second thief pays him כפל.

steps.title: רב ששת says רב gave this ruling while half-asleep
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת rejects רב's ruling. He says רב must have said it while drowsy and lying down.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: I say that רב said this teaching when he was sleepy and lying down.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת attacks רב's ruling strongly. He says it does not hold up. His proof comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying רב was 'dozing' is a sharp way of saying the ruling was not thought through. רב ששת is challenging רב's main idea that יאוש lets the first thief acquire the stolen item.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said: I say
that when Rav was dozing and lying down
he said this teaching.
phrases.notes: In other words, רב did not think this ruling through.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: אָמֵינָא כִּי נָיֵים וְשָׁכֵיב רַב אָמַר לְהָא שְׁמַעְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's ruling from step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that after יאוש the first thief acquires the item and the second thief pays him כפל.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב ששת holds the ruling is wrong, and he will try to prove it from a ברייתא.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: four or five times because he sank deeper into sin
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת brings a ברייתא. רבי עקיבא explains that a thief who slaughters or sells pays four or five times because he became more rooted in the sin.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: רבי עקיבא said: Why did the Torah say that if he slaughtered or sold he pays four or five times? Because he became deeply rooted in the sin.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת brings a ברייתא as the source for his attack on רב. Here he only quotes it. He has not yet used it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא gives a reason for the four- and five-times payment. By slaughtering or selling, the thief went further and became more rooted in his sin. רב ששת will use this reason to ask when the sale took place.

keyTerms.meaning: He became deeply rooted in sin

phrases.english: As it was taught: Rabbi Akiva said:
For what reason did the Torah say
that if he slaughtered or sold
he pays the fourfold or fivefold payment?
Because he became deeply rooted in the sin.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: מִפְּנֵי מָה אָמְרָה תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source behind רב ששת's attack in step 26.
steps.raayaObject: That רב is wrong about יאוש making the stolen item belong to the thief.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי עקיבא's ברייתא explaining that the four- and five-times payment comes because the thief became rooted in sin.

steps.title: When did the sale happen? First option: before יאוש
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת asks when the slaughtering or selling in רבי עקיבא's case took place. He begins with the option that it was before יאוש.
steps.simpleTranslation: When did this happen? If you say before the owner gave up hope,
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת starts to analyze the ברייתא by asking when the sale happened. He opens with the first option, before יאוש, and the argument continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question about timing is how רב ששת will use רבי עקיבא's reason against רב. By checking each option, before יאוש and after יאוש, he plans to show what יאוש does and does not do. Here we only see him begin the first option.

phrases.english: When?
phrases.notes: He is asking when the thief in רבי עקיבא's case slaughtered or sold the animal.

phrases.english: If you say before despair,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins using the ברייתא from step 27 against רב.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the slaughtering or selling in רבי עקיבא's case happened before or after the owner's יאוש.
